title: Samaria, Simon the Sorcerer, and the Ethiopian
summary: After Stephen's death a great persecution, led by Saul, scatters the church through Judea and Samaria, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria with signs and great joy; many are baptized, including the sorcerer Simon, and when Peter and John come and lay hands on the Samaritans they receive the Holy Spirit. Simon tries to buy that power and is rebuked. Then an angel sends Philip to the desert road, where he explains Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official and baptizes him.
story: Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and then to the ends of the earth (1:8). Chapter 8 begins the second stage. The trigger is suffering: Stephen's death and Saul's persecution drive believers out of Jerusalem, and they take the word with them. Two boundary crossings follow. The first is to the Samaritans, a people Jews regarded as heretical half-relatives. The second is to an African court official, a eunuch who could not enter the inner courts of the temple, returning to a kingdom at the southern edge of the known world. The chapter prepares for the conversion of Saul in chapter 9 and the opening to Gentiles in chapter 10.
historical:
The Samaritans lived in the central hill country between Judea and Galilee. Their origins were bitterly disputed. Second Kings 17 describes how the Assyrians, after taking Samaria in 722 BC, settled foreign peoples in the land who mixed the worship of the LORD with other gods. The Samaritans themselves claimed descent from the northern tribes of Israel. They accepted only the five books of Moses, worshiped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem, and looked for a coming prophet like Moses. Their temple on Gerizim was destroyed by the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus in the late second century BC, which deepened the hostility (compare John 4:9, 20).

The queen called Candace ruled the kingdom of Kush (called Ethiopia by Greeks and Romans), centered on the city of Meroë on the Nile in what is now Sudan, not modern Ethiopia. Candace was a title for the queen mother, who held real power there, rather than a personal name. The road from Jerusalem to Gaza led toward the coast and then Egypt. Azotus is the old Philistine city of Ashdod, and Caesarea was the Roman administrative capital on the coast, where Philip later lived with his four daughters (21:8-9).
cultural:
Magic and sorcery were widespread in the ancient world. Practitioners claimed power over spirits and fate, sold spells and charms, and sometimes presented themselves as divine. Simon's title, the Great Power, suggests he claimed to embody a divine force. Second-century Christian writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus describe a Simon of Samaria as a founder of heretical movements, though whether all their stories concern the same man is uncertain. The English word simony, the buying or selling of church offices, comes from him.

The Ethiopian official was a eunuch, a castrated man, which was common for officials serving royal women. Deuteronomy 23:1 barred such men from the assembly of the LORD, and he would have been restricted in the temple even if he was a convert or a God-fearer. Yet Isaiah 56:3-5, a few chapters after the passage he was reading, promises eunuchs who keep God's covenant a name better than sons and daughters. Reading aloud was the normal practice in the ancient world, which is how Philip could hear him. Owning a scroll of Isaiah was a mark of wealth and devotion.
literary: The chapter has three scenes: the persecution and scattering (1-4), Philip in Samaria, including Simon and the apostles' visit (5-25), and Philip with the Ethiopian (26-40). Both of Philip's missions are guided by God, the second explicitly by an angel and the Spirit. The Ethiopian scene is carefully built: a question (Do you understand?), an answer (How can I, unless someone guides me?), a Scripture (Isaiah 53:7-8), a question about it (who is the prophet talking about?), the gospel beginning from that text, and baptism. Many readers compare it with the road to Emmaus in Luke 24, where Jesus opens the Scriptures to two travelers. Verse 37, a confession of faith before baptism, appears in some later manuscripts but not in the earliest, and most modern translations omit it or place it in a footnote.

outline.t: Persecution scatters the church; the word spreads
Simon the sorcerer believes and is baptized
Peter and John: the Samaritans receive the Spirit
Simon tries to buy the gift of God
Philip and the Ethiopian reading Isaiah
The Ethiopian's baptism; Philip carried away

doctrines.note: The gospel crosses its first great boundaries: to Samaritans, long despised by Jews, and to an African eunuch excluded from full participation in temple worship. Persecution meant to stop the church becomes the means of its spread. The chapter shows the mission driven by God, who sends and guides his witnesses.

The Samaritans believe and are baptized but receive the Spirit only when Peter and John lay hands on them. Christians interpret this delay differently (see the hard question), but all agree that it united the Samaritan believers with the apostles in Jerusalem so that there would be one church, not two rival ones.

Baptism follows faith in both scenes: the Samaritans are baptized when they believe the gospel, and the Ethiopian asks to be baptized after hearing it. The account does not settle debates about the mode or subjects of baptism, but it shows baptism as the immediate response of faith.
The gift of God cannot be bought with money. Simon wanted spiritual power as a commodity, and Peter's rebuke is fierce. Salvation and the Spirit are received, not purchased or controlled.

words.note: Eunouchos, eunuch. The word could sometimes be used for a high official without implying castration, but Luke uses it five times in this passage, suggesting that the man's status matters to the story. His inclusion fulfills Isaiah 56's promise that eunuchs who hold fast to God's covenant will not be cut off.

Dorea, gift, a free gift. Peter calls the Holy Spirit the gift of God (8:20), the same word he used at Pentecost for the gift of the Holy Spirit (2:38). The word stresses that the Spirit is given freely, which is exactly why he cannot be bought.

Euangelizomai, to announce good news, from which comes the word evangelize. It appears repeatedly in this chapter: the scattered believers, Philip, Peter and John all preach the good news. The good news is Jesus himself (8:35), and it is announced to Samaritans and to an Ethiopian as freely as to Jews in Jerusalem.

christ: Philip proclaims the Christ in Samaria and preaches the good news about Jesus to the Ethiopian, beginning with Isaiah 53. That passage, one of the servant songs, describes one who is led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent before his accusers, humiliated and deprived of justice, whose life is taken from the earth. The Ethiopian's question, whether the prophet speaks of himself or someone else, is still asked; Jewish interpreters have often read the servant as Israel or a righteous figure within Israel. Philip, like the whole New Testament, reads it as fulfilled in Jesus, who suffered silently and was put to death for the sins of others. The chapter shows the crucified and risen Christ drawing to himself those at the margins: Samaritans, a sorcerer called to repentance, and a foreign eunuch who goes on his way rejoicing.

hard.q: Why did the Samaritans receive the Spirit only after the apostles came, when Acts 2:38 links the Spirit with repentance and baptism?
hard.a:
This is one of the most debated passages in Acts, and each tradition reads it in light of its own practice. Pentecostal Christians often see here a baptism in the Spirit that comes after conversion as a second experience, a pattern they find elsewhere in Acts. Catholic, Orthodox, and some Anglican Christians have often seen in the laying on of hands a basis for confirmation (or chrismation), in which the Spirit's gift is sealed through the church's ministers.

Many evangelical and Reformed interpreters see the delay as exceptional, tied to the unique moment when the gospel first crossed into Samaria. On this view God withheld the Spirit until the apostles came so that the Samaritan believers would be joined to the Jerusalem church and the old division between Jews and Samaritans would not reappear inside the church. Some scholars, such as James Dunn in Baptism in the Holy Spirit (1970), argued instead that the Samaritans' first faith was deficient, as Simon's clearly was, and that they truly came to faith only later. Acts itself shows no single fixed order: the Spirit comes before baptism in chapter 10, after baptism here, and with laying on of hands in chapter 19. These are second-order questions, and faithful churches differ.

questions: Persecution scattered the church, and the scattered believers preached wherever they went. How has hardship pushed you into places you would not otherwise have gone?
Simon wanted spiritual power he could control. In what subtle ways do people try to buy or manage God's gifts today?
The Ethiopian said, How can I understand unless someone guides me? Who has guided you in reading Scripture, and whom might you guide?
